"If you work there, you must earn a lot of money." Kingsley spoke up. "Actually, that is where | met Pat. Before | got back my family's fortune, | worked at Helix for a while. And Pat and Celeste are the founders. So they are the top dogs." My mother gasped. "Pat, you are literally swimming in money right now!" My father jumped in. "Pat, your sister does not really have a job right now.

Since you have such a big position in such a big lab, why not find a vacancy for your sister Vivian?" | turned to look at Vivian, who was staring at me with so much hatred | could feel it burning across the table. "I am sorry. | actually cannot help her. Except for someone who has a lot of experience, only people with doctorates are allowed to work there. You can ask Kingsley. Even he is a PhD holder." Kingsley nodded. The color drained from Vivian's face as the implication of my words sank in. | had not meant them as a shade, but now | realized how they sounded.

My sister had gotten pregnant early, out of wedlock. She had been just about to begin college when she got pregnant, so she had ended up marrying Jonathan. She never pursued her education after that. They had always mocked me for it, the fact that | went to school and poured my time and passion into my career. But now, it felt really good. As though Kingsley sensed something from the way everyone had gone quiet, he suddenly spoke. "Actually, getting an education is really important." He turned to look directly at Vivian. "I think it is not too late for you to go back to school."

chapters.title: Chapter 393
chapters.content:
Chapter 393 His gaze lingered on her as he continued. "A woman should have a career. It is very important in life. | mean, look at Pat. At her age, she is successful. She is a boss. She has a lot of money. She is not lacking for anything. Even Pat's best friend, Celeste, the one who was present when the five billion was invested into Helix, she also went to school. She made a name for herself. Look at what she and Pat are accomplishing. That is how a woman should be. That is how much a woman should be passionate about having her own career.

If a woman does not go to school, does not have a job, what exactly is she doing with her life?" Kingsley was saying all of this deliberately. | was sure of it now. Could it be that he already understood how my family treated me? Did someone tell him about it? Celeste was not such a talkative person. | decided | would have to ask her when | left here. Vivian could not take it anymore. She got up and excused herself, saying she was going to the restroom. The moment she left, my mother began to act so sweet it made my stomach turn. She picked up a plate and began scooping food onto it.

"You look so malnourished, Pat. Come and eat." Something about the act made me feel even more sick. | did not know if it was the food getting to me, or the pretense | could no longer put up with, but | got up as well. "| need to use the restroom." | walked quickly, and the moment the door closed behind me, | ran to the toilet and threw up. | washed myself, breathing hard, and when | came out, Vivian was waiting for me at the door. "| know what you did today." Her voice was low and mocking. "All of that was just to make a comeback, right?" | stared at her.

"No matter how much you try to act like you are better than me, you will never have what | have." She stepped closer, her smile sharp as glass. "Of course, you could go to school. You could bring a man like Kingsley to show up. But everyone knows that engagement is not marriage. | know for a fact that all of this is just for show, just to deceive our parents. And all those gifts, they mean nothing. What matters is having a stable family. That is something | have. | have a husband. | have children. But look at you, Pat. You let yourself go. You are old already.

And there is a possibility you will never become a mother in this life. You can never measure up to me, Pat, no matter how much education you acquire." | smiled. Then | covered my mouth as though | was about to throw up. Vivian stepped back, her nose wrinkling. "Gross. What do you think you are doing?" "Sorry." | lowered my hand. "I think the baby in my womb disagrees with what you just said." "What?" "Come on, is it not obvious?" | tilted my head. "I thought it was obvious.

| mean, for someone like you who has had three children, | thought you would be able to tell that there is something different about me. There is a child in my womb. A tiny little baby growing there." Vivian stared at me, her face running through a dozen expressions in the span of a second, shock winning out in the end. She could not form a single word. Eventually, she turned and walked away. | stood there for a while, breathing heavily. Then regret hit me. | had let Vivian provoke me into mentioning my baby, something | had planned to keep secret.

| had not wanted to tell anyone until | was ready. | cursed under my breath. | took a few more minutes to calm myself before | went back. The moment | walked into the room and headed for my seat, Vivian's voice rang out, loud and clear. "Mom, has Pat told you that she is pregnant?" There was silence. Every pair of eyes swung to me. | stood frozen by my chair, the ring on my finger suddenly heavy, the secret ripped open for the whole table to feast on. Vivian smiled at me from across the room, sweet and venomous.

chapters.title: Chapter 394
chapters.content:
Chapter 394 The silence around that table lasted three heartbeats, and then my mother's voice cut through it like a blade. "Pat. Is it true? Are you really pregnant?" Her hands shook where they lay on the tablecloth, and her voice trembled on the last word. | looked at Vivian, at the smile she was no longer bothering to hide behind her hand, and | felt the trap close around me. Every pair of eyes in the room pressed down on my shoulders, Kingsley's among them, wide and unreadable. | wanted to say no. But! could not. The child was real, and | was not ready to spend the cost of the lie.

"Yes, Mom." My voice came out steadier than | expected. "I'm pregnant with Kingsley's baby. | was planning to share the news with all of you after the wedding, but | guess Vivian beat me to it." My mother burst into tears. Not the practiced, delicate tears Vivian had cried over the necklace. Real ones, fat and streaming, her hands flying to her mouth as she stared at me like | had handed her the moon. Then she was on her feet, around the table, pulling me into her arms and sobbing into my hair. "Oh, Pat. This is the best day of my life." She pulled back, cupped my face in her wet hands.

"It has always been my dream to see your baby, to hold my grandchild from you. | always knew you were destined for greatness, even when you were still a little girl. And look at you now. You're perfect. You have a career, you have an amazing husband, and now a baby on the way. All that's left is the wedding. Every mother deserves a child like you." "A boy or a girl, Pat?" my aunt called out, beaming. "Have you picked a name yet?" my uncle added. "Congratulations, dear! We always knew you would do well," a distant cousin | barely recognized chimed in.

They crowded around, all talking at once, congratulating me like they had never said a single cruel word about my life, like the past hour had not happened at all. Even my father dabbed at his eyes with a napkin. | could not take it anymore. | opened my mouth to say something, anything, but Kingsley spoke first. "Actually, | would have to leave." "Really?" My mother's face crumpled. "So soon?" "Yes." | found my voice before Kingsley could. "We actually have some plans. | didn't expect this party to take so long, I've already spent too much time here.

| need to stop at the lab, and Kingsley and | have things to take care of too." "Call us, Pat!" my mother called as we reached the door. "Come back before the wedding, both of you!" my father added. "You must bring Kingsley to dinner!" my aunt shouted after us, waving. | zoned out most of it and quietly walked out. | breathed in deep, the cool breeze outside washing over my face, and | was aware of Kingsley walking behind me, his footsteps steady on the gravel. | did not bother to say a word to him. | went straight to my car, and | was about to get in when his voice stopped me.

: "Hold on, Pat. We need to talk." | turned and stared at him for a long moment. Then | opened the door, got in, and started the engine. He walked around the other side and got in as well, leaving his car behind. "Drive somewhere," he said. "Wherever you'll be comfortable. Let's stop." | began to drive. | was hungry. It was way past lunchtime, and | had not had an appetite earlier in the day, so | pulled up in front of a quiet restaurant and walked in. Kingsley followed silently behind me. | sat down at a corner table and looked around for a waiter, and that was when he spoke.

"So, Pat." His voice was low, careful. "You're pregnant with my child?" "No." | kept my eyes on the menu, on words | was not reading. "Yes, | was pregnant. But | had an abortion." "What?" His voice cracked through the quiet restaurant, loud enough that heads turned. | looked up and met his eyes, and | watched the color drain out of his face.

chapters.title: Chapter 395
chapters.content:
Chapter 395 "Why? Why would you do that?" He caught the stares then, looked around, and lowered his voice. "Let's talk outside." | sighed, got up, and went out. He followed, and once we were on the pavement he pulled me to the side, away from the windows, his hand tight on my arm. "What did you say, Pat?" His voice shook. "You got rid of my child? Without even asking me? Why? How could you do something so cruel?" "| never planned for any of it to happen." | kept my voice even, though something in my chest was twisting. "And the day | found out, | just panicked.

| know you don't love me, and | didn't want the fact that we have a child together to force a situation where we would have to end up together. | didn't want you trying to be with me out of obligation. So | got rid of the child, because | wouldn't stay with a man who doesn't love me." Kingsley stared at me, and | could see he was visibly upset. His hands shook at his sides. His eyes turned red, so red that tears almost spilled out, and when he spoke again his voice was thick and raw. "How could you do such a thing? That child was innocent. That was my child. My baby had every right to live.

And | had every right to decide what would happen with the child. You had no right to get rid of it without telling me." Seeing the tears in his eyes, | suddenly felt guilty for lying to him. | had thought he would not really care about the child, that it would be nothing to him but an inconvenience. But the grief breaking across his face was real, and | knew I had been wrong. | sighed. Even if we did not end up together, | could at least tell him the truth "Actually, | had just begun..." "Oh my God!

Kingsley!" A bright voice cut through the air, and | turned to see a tall girl with slender legs, beautiful and polished, running toward us across the pavement. She threw herself into Kingsley's arms, her face buried in his chest, and Kingsley stood there as though he was in shock, his hands frozen at his sides, unable to move. The girl hugged him for a long time. When she finally pulled away, she turned to me and smiled, a smile that did not quite reach her eyes. "Hi! Um, wow. Okay, sorry, sorry. | must have intruded on your conversation, but I'll just introduce myself.

My name is Sharon, and I'm Kingsley's fiancée. The love of his life." | stood there, watching the scene in front of me like I was watching a movie that had nothing to do with me. Then | chuckled. Of course. Why should this surprise me? This was exactly why | had tried to protect myself, why | had never let myself believe in the kneeling and the pretty words and the ring. | refused to allow myself to get hurt by things like this. Kingsley still stood there, frozen, and | took out the ring he had given me, and extended it toward him.

He did not move, so | took his palm, opened it, and placed the ring init. The weight of it snapped him back. He stared at the ring in his palm, then pulled his arm away from the girl who said she was Sharon. "What are you doing, Pat? What is all this?" He turned to look at the girl, then turned back to me. "Listen, listen. This is not what it looks like. | know what you're thinking. "No, it's fine." My voice came out calm, almost kind. "I know exactly what this looks like. The truth is, Kingsley, | cannot do this, okay?" | turned and walked away.

He called after me, tried to follow, but | did not stop. | kept walking until | reached my car, got in, and drove away. | drove for a while with no destination, the streets sliding past in a blur, and then | pulled over and took a deep breath. My heart was pounding.

chapters.title: Chapter 396
chapters.content:
Chapter 396 Tears gathered at the corners of my eyes as | thought about everything Kingsley had done, the way he had knelt in front of my whole family and looked at me like | was the only woman in the world. And then the girl, beautiful and polished, throwing herself into his arms, calling herself the love of his life. I smiled and wiped my eyes. Of course, Pat. You already knew how everything would end from the very beginning. Don't let this bother you. | continued driving until | arrived at Helix. | parked my car, got out, and began to walk toward the building.

According to the plan with Celeste, | was not supposed to go to Helix. | was supposed to go home after the party. But | just wanted to be with someone dear. | wanted to be with Celeste, to talk to her about how | felt. | did not want to go home and be all alone. "Hey. Stop right there." A female voice spoke from behind me. | stopped and turned. It was Sharon, the same girl from before, walking toward me with her chin lifted and her eyes blazing. She came close, close enough that | caught her perfume, and she pointed her finger at me. "I'm warning you." Her voice was sharp and sweet at once.

"Kingsley and | have been together since university. We are so much in love that he cannot even breathe a single breath without me. If you have a mirror, you should take a good look at yourself, because you do not even come close. Look at me. Look at how beautiful I am. Look at how handsome Kingsley is. We are perfect for each other." | watched her quietly, without wasting a single word in response. She kept talking, her mouth opening and closing, spitting insults. "You think a man like him would ever look twice at someone like you? You're old. You're plain. You're nothing.

Stay far away from my man, or you will regret the day you were born." She kept talking and talking and talking, and the words washed over me like noise. And just as the last word left her mouth, someone appeared from behind me and gave her a hard slap across her face. "Who the hell do you think you are?" I turned and saw Celeste. 2 She stood there, her hand still raised, her eyes blazing with fury, and | let out a breath | had not known | was holding. Sharon held her cheek, her eyes wide with shock. " Celeste? You? How dare you raise a hand to my face, Celeste?

How dare you?" "Get off my property right now," Celeste said, her voice low and dangerous, "or things will get really ugly for you, Sharon. Get out, right now!" Sharon stared at Celeste with so much anger, her jaw working, her cheek already reddening. "You have no idea what you have just done, Celeste. This is not over. This is definitely not over." She turned and walked away, her heels clicking sharp and fast on the concrete. + Celeste stood there, her fists balled at her sides, shaking with rage, her eyes burning holes in the space where Sharon had been.

Watching her, | realized something was wrong, and it might not even have anything to do with me. I stayed where | was for a while, watching her breathe. Then, without saying anything, | moved closer and pulled her into my arms, hugging her tight. "Whatever it is, Celeste, it's fine." | spoke against her hair. "It's okay. Just calm down. We can talk about it." : Just then, | heard a cough behind me. Then Kingsley's voice. 5 "Have | come at a bad time?"

chapters.title: Chapter 397
chapters.content:
Chapter 397 SPARROW I walked out of the Beaumont hotel with Tasha trailing behind me like a ghost, her footsteps so soft on the floor that | almost forgot she was there. The car sat where | had left it, black and gleaming under the hotel awning, and | slid into the driver's seat while she climbed in on the passenger side with the care of someone afraid of breaking something. The door closed with a click. Then silence. | pulled out of the lot and onto the main road, and that was when | noticed her hands.

They were shaking in her lap, fingers twisting together like she was trying to wring water out of them. She had not looked at me once since we left the penthouse. Her eyes stayed fixed on the window, on her lap, anywhere but on me. | could not understand it. | had been good to her. Better than good. | had pulled her out of a life that was slowly killing her, promised to handle the man who had been poisoning her, handed her a future she could not have imagined a week ago. | was doing things for her and her aunt that | would not do for anyone on this earth, and she knew it.

So why did she sit there trembling like | was the danger she had been running from? If she had been any other woman, | might have assumed she was playing a part, performing fear because she thought it was what | wanted. But Tasha was not clever enough for that kind of game. This was genuine terror, rolling off her in waves so thick | could nearly taste it. The whole thing was a turn-off. Completely. Even if | had been interested in taking her to my bed, this wimpish cowering would have killed the thought stone dead. | did not want a woman who flinched when | moved.

| wanted someone with spine, someone with teeth, someone who would bite back and enjoy it. Someone like her aunt. : | pushed the thought away before it could take root and kept driving. could put out with a text. Every few minutes | glanced up and caught Tasha disappearing into the dressing room or emerging from it, always with that same frightened look on her face, like a fawn being dressed by wolves. Then she came out for the last time, and | understood why the manager had been smiling. The transformation was simple, and simple was exactly what made it perfect.

A long white dress that fell to her ankles, modest in every way that mattered, cut to make her look like she had been poured out of morning light. The heavy makeup was gone, her face clean and fresh, her skin glowing the way skin did when it had never known a lifetime of paint. Her hair had been styled into something soft and plain, the kind of hairstyle a man imagined on the girl he brought home to his mother. The old hag would eat this up. She would look at Tasha and see everything she wanted for a granddaughter in- law; a good girl, an innocent girl, a bride out of a storybook.

+ I took Tasha's hand. She startled at the touch but did not pull away, and | examined her fingers, small, delicate, unadorned. | scanned the glass case beside us and dismissed the diamonds immediately. Diamonds were loud, flashy, the kind of stone a woman picked for herself. For the image | needed, nothing said quiet virtue like gold. Simple. Warm. Unassuming. not pull away, and | examined her fingers, small, delicate, unadorned. | scanned the glass case beside us and dismissed the diamonds immediately. Diamonds were loud, flashy, the kind of stone a woman picked for herself.

For the image | needed, nothing said quiet virtue like gold. Simple. Warm. Unassuming.

chapters.title: Chapter 398
chapters.content:
Chapter 398 | chose a slim gold band, the kind that looked like it had been in the family for generations, and held it out to her. "Your engagement ring." She looked at the ring, then at me, and | watched her throat work before she took it from my palm. "Thank you, "she murmured, and slid it onto her finger without meeting my eyes. It fit perfectly. Of course it did. | paid, tipped enough to make the manager's eyes go wide, and led Tasha out of the boutique.

The drive to the mansion took us through streets that grew cleaner and quieter the closer we came, the houses growing larger and more guarded until the city itself seemed to hold its breath. The mansion rose up ahead, white and sprawling, my grandmother's territory now, though it had once belonged to a man who was more brother to me than blood. | parked and turned to Tasha before she could reach for the door. "Be respectful. Smile kindly at her. Do not upset her. Whatever she asks, answer sweetly, and leave the rest tome." She nodded, her fingers already finding each other again.

"If all goes well tonight, the old hag will have no reason to interfere in my life ever again." Granny was in the sitting room when we entered, and the look on her face when she saw Tasha was almost worth the drive. Shock, pure and simple, her mouth opening and closing like a fish that had just been told the ocean was closing. She had clearly expected me to arrive alone, had probably convinced herself that the fiancée | had mentioned was a convenient fiction, a lie to get her off my back. Imelda was there too, dressed in a white dress of her own, her face painted with makeup.

She was a pretty woman in her own right, but standing next to Tasha she faded like a candle in sunlight. Her reaction was nothing like the old woman's. Imelda's face lit up with something that looked like pure relief, and she practically flew across the room, wrapping Tasha in a hug and welcoming her to the house like a long-lost sister. Tasha gave her a warm smile, and Imelda beamed, and then she disappeared into her room and did not come out again. | could not say | blamed her. None of this had been her choice either.

| apologized to Granny for being five minutes late and she barely acknowledged it, her eyes fixed on Tasha like she was trying to read a language she had never learned. She studied her for a long moment, and | watched the suspicion drain out of her face. Tasha stood there fidgeting, her shoulders tight, looking so nervous that | almost felt sorry for her. Perhaps the old woman felt it too, because something in her expression softened, and she smiled, a real smile, not the tight-lipped one she wore when she was about †o lecture me. "Come, child." She held out her hand. "Sit down.

It is already time for dinner, and | have been waiting for you. | did not know what you liked, so | made sure many dishes were prepared. You must be hungry." Tasha smiled shyly, her voice small and sweet. "Thank you, Grandmother." | hid a smile of my own. The girl could act when she had to. The old woman beamed. "Grandmother. | like that. Come, sit." Over the first course, Granny asked the question | had been waiting for, the one that would make or break the performance. "So tell me, child." She set down her spoon and fixed Tasha with a warm look. "How did you meet my grandson?

| know Sparrow is a busy man. He barely has time for me, and | am his own grandmother. How did a delicate flower like you manage to catch his eye?" Tasha's face went white, like someone had drained the color out of her with a tap. Her mouth opened and closed, and | could see the panic building behind her eyes, the complete absence of an answer. | set down my glass and spoke before the silence could stretch into suspicion. "The memory is a little painful for her, Granny. Perhaps | should tell it." The old woman's brows rose, but she nodded.

| sorted the details like a deck of cards and dealt them out one by one. "Tasha was desperate when | met her. Her only surviving relative, her mother, was dying. She had taken ajob at a hotel as a waitress, working herself to the bone to pay for treatment, but her manager was a vile man. He made advances at her, and when she refused, he made her life a misery. He bullied her daily, withheld her pay, threatened her job whenever she complained."

chapters.title: Chapter 399
chapters.content:
Chapter 399 | paused, letting the weight of it settle over the table. "| was passing by the hotel one evening and heard a commotion in the back. The man had cornered her, and she was crying. | normally mind my own business, it is a rule | live by, but | could not overlook such injustice, not when she was weeping like that. | stepped in. | had the man fired for his behavior, and when | looked into it, | discovered he had been blocking Tasha's pay the entire time, leaving her mother's treatment in a critical condition." Granny's hand had come to rest over her heart.

"It was too late by the time | intervened." | let my voice drop. "Her mother died that same day. Tasha had no one left. Since then, | have been the only family she has." I reached across the table and took Tasha's hand. She flinched, barely, but | held on, gently, and looked at Granny with what | hoped read as quiet devotion. "Tasha is very important to me. | kept her a secret all this time because she is shy, innocent, and | did not want anyone troubling her. She has been through enough." The silence that followed was thick with sympathy.

Granny looked at Tasha with such pity in her eyes that | almost felt guilty for the fiction. When | glanced at Tasha, she was staring at me with wide eyes, her mouth slightly open, and | could read the thought on her face as clearly as if she had spoken it aloud. She could not believe how good a liar | was. | squeezed her hand and smiled at her like a devoted fiancé. She looked away. The old woman rose from her seat, came around the table, and took Tasha's hands in her own, pulling her gently to her feet. "Listen to me, child." Her voice was thick with emotion.

" You can consider me your family from now on. | will always support you, no matter the circumstances. Do you hear me? Always." Tasha's chin trembled. And then, to my genuine surprise, she began to cry. Real tears, streaming down her cheeks, her shoulders shaking with silent sobs. | stared at her, caught off guard. Was this real, or was she performing? | could not tell, and | prided myself on being able to tell. The girl had more layers than | had given her credit for.

Granny pulled her into a hug, patting her back and murmuring soothing words, and | sat there watching the two of them, waiting for the drama to play out. It went on for a while, the old woman loved a good cry, and Tasha seemed to have an endless supply of tears. Eventually Tasha sniffled her way back to calm, and Granny wiped her cheeks with a handkerchief and smiled at her like she was already a granddaughter. "Come." Granny patted her hand. "Let us eat. You must keep up your strength." The rest of the meal went better than | had dared to hope.

Granny was pleased, | could see it in the way she kept glancing at Tasha, in the way she piled food onto her plate, in the way she smiled every time Tasha called her Grandmother. "You have good taste, Sparrow." She nodded approvingly at one point. "I like her. She is a good girl. You must take care of her always. Do you hear me?" "| hear you, Granny." | meant it more than she knew. The conversation drifted to safer waters; the house, the weather, the latest gossip from the circles Granny still moved in, and I let it wash over me, contributing just enough to seem engaged.

Then Granny set down her fork and fixed me with a look. "So when is the wedding?" | did not blink. "In a few days." Her fork clattered against the plate. "A few days? Sparrow, that is hardly any time at all. | thought it was a joke. Are you certain?" "Lam certain." She stared at me for a long moment, then broke into a smile. "Well. | would not miss it for the world. | will be there, front row, with bells on." "| would expect nothing less, Granny." She turned to Tasha, her eyes bright. "| have some ideas for the wedding, child.

| hope you do not mind an old woman sticking her nose in." Tasha smiled, and there was something almost genuine in it. "1 will follow whatever you think is best, Grandmother."

chapters.title: Chapter 400
chapters.content:
Chapter 400 The old woman positively glowed. The doorbell rang while Granny was describing the exact shade of cream roses she had in mind for the centerpieces, and she paused mid-sentence, frowning. "lam not expecting anyone else." "| will check." | walked to the door, silent on the floor, and peered through the peephole. For a moment | thought | was seeing things. Scarlett stood on the doorstep, flanked by Jasmine and Maya, all three poured into clothes that left very little to the imagination. Scarlett's was hugging every curve like it had been painted on.

Jasmine's was black and shorter than my patience. Even Maya, who usually dressed like she wanted to disappear, had been squeezed into something that showed more skin than fabric. | opened the door, and for a long moment we simply stared at each other. "Where is my Tasha?" Scarlett demanded, and there was steel in her voice | had not heard before. | should have been annoyed. Instead, | was impressed. She had tracked me here, which meant she had either followed me from the boutique or worked out my location from the city's surveillance.

Either way, it was more resourcefulness than most of my enemies could boast, and she was doing it in heels and a dress. | could not leave them standing on the doorstep. The old hag would be deeply displeased by the way they were dressed, but leaving them outside would draw more attention than letting them in, and this street had neighbors with nothing better to do than gossip. "Come in," | said, stepping aside. "Tasha!" Scarlett exclaimed the moment she saw her niece, her face splitting into a smile, and she started across the room with her arms already open.

Tasha was getting to her feet, her face lighting up, and that was when Granny's voice cut through the room like a blade. "Who are these prostitutes?" Scarlett froze mid-step. Jasmine and Maya froze behind her. The three of them stood there, caught in the headlights of the old woman's disdain, and | watched the realization dawn on their faces, that this was not a casual gathering, that the woman before them was my grandmother, that the dinner they had interrupted was a carefully staged performance with Tasha as the star. "lam so sorry, ma'am.

We..." Scarlett's voice shifted into something smooth and contrite. | cut her off. "Granny, these are the girls who worked with Tasha at the hotel. They were good to her." Tasha caught my drift faster than | expected. "Yes, Grandmother." Her voice came out bright and innocent." They are my friends from work. Actually, | mentioned to them earlier that | was having dinner with my fiancé and his grandmother, and..." "So they decided to show up uninvited and gatecrash our dinner." Granny finished the sentence for her, her voice flat. Tasha swallowed.

Scarlett recovered quickly, a smile sliding onto her face like a mask. "We were visiting someone in the neighborhood. We were just leaving when we remembered our friend was having dinner here, and we decided to stop by and say hello." The old woman laughed, a short, humorless sound, and then her expression curdled into disgust. "How convenient." She turned to Tasha, picked up the serving spoon, and piled more food onto her plate, her voice softening into something almost maternal. "Child, you must be wary of the kind of people you keep as friends. Some of them are jealous.

They want what you have. They would do anything to seduce your man, including showing up uninvited to a dinner clearly meant for three, dressed like cheap prostitutes." Tasha nodded, her eyes downcast. "Yes, Grandmother." I turned to look at Scarlett. Her expression had not changed, she still wore that polite, pleasant smile, as though Granny had been discussing the weather. Not a flicker of hurt, not a hint of anger. | felt a strange sense of relief, though | could not have said why it mattered to me. But the old hag was not finished.

Chapter 418 | paused, letting the weight of it settle. "| am telling you this because | believe you are a man who can do something about it. Pat will be going there tomorrow. If you truly care about her, this is your chance to be her knight in shining armor. Show up, Kingsley. Stand beside her. Let her family see, for once in her life, what she is worth." "Do you have the address?" "| will send it to you in the morning." "Send it tonight." His voice was tight now, all that careful calm burned away. "I do not want to waste a single hour | could be using to prepare." I smiled to myself.

"Very well. The address will be in your phone before you wake up." "Celeste." He said my name like he was making a vow Thank you. | will not let her down. | swear to you, | will not let her down." "See that you do not. Good night, Kingsley." "Good night." | ended the call and sat there for a moment, the phone warm in my hand, thinking about how much | had just gambled on a man who had once broken my best friend. But | had heard the truth in his voice, and | believed that a man could be the worst thing that ever happened to someone and still spend the rest of his life trying to be the best.

| did not tell him about the pregnancy. That was not my secret to tell. Pat would share it when she was ready, and | would be standing behind her when she did. | checked the time and opened my phone to call Dominic, and that was when | heard the click of the lock and the soft swing of the front door. | was off the bed before | knew | had moved, crossing the room and down the stairs, and there he was, shrugging out of his jacket, tired lines around his eyes, and the sight of him undid something in me | had not known was wound so tight.

| threw myself at him, and he caught me with a laugh that turned into an oomph as my arms locked around his neck. "You missed me that much?" "Shut up." | buried my face in his shoulder and breathed him in. He smelled like airports and old money and the particular warmth that was just him. "How was the flight?" "Long." His arms tightened around my waist. "Two hours there, two hours back, and | spent every minute of it wishing you were in the seat next to me." | pulled back just enough to look at him, and his eyes were soft and tired and full of something that made my chest ache.

| kissed him, slow and deep, and his hand came up to cup the back of my head, and for a long moment the whole world narrowed to the warmth of his mouth and the steady beat of his heart under my palm. "How are you?" he asked against my lips. "1 am fine. Better now." "And Pat?" "Resting. She fell asleep a while ago. The soup did her good." He smiled and pressed his forehead to mine. "| am glad she is settling in." "You must be exhausted. Go shower, and | will heat something up for you." He raised an eyebrow, a hint of mischief cutting through the tiredness.

"| have been gone for hours, and the first thing you want me to do is shower?" "The second thing." | patted his chest and stepped back. "The first thing was the kiss. Now go, before you fall asleep standing up." He laughed and headed upstairs, and | went to the kitchen and put together a proper meal, something warm and quick, and by the time he came down in a fresh shirt with damp hair he was already looking more human. We sat across from each other at the marble island, and | watched him eat for a while before | asked the question that had been sitting on my tongue since he walked in.

chapters.title: Chapter 419
chapters.content:
Chapter 419 "How did it go with Imelda's father?" A slow smile spread across his face, the kind of smile a man wears when he has just won a war without firing a shot. "Imelda will no longer be a name that inconveniences either of us. Not after tomorrow morning." "What did you do?" "| apologized to her father." He set down his fork. "I took the blame. | told him | should have been clearer with my grandmother from the beginning, that | let the situation fester until his daughter was dragged across the world on a promise that was never mine to make. And then | told him the truth.

That even if | married Imelda, she would never be happy, because she would never have my love. | would give her my name, my money, my protection, everything a woman could ask for, except the one thing that matters, and | would be doing her a great cruelty to pretend otherwise." | nodded slowly. "And he accepted that?" "He did." Dominic's eyes gleamed. "Because | did not leave it at words. | offered him a deal as compensation. A business acquisition | had been working on for weeks, worth billions. | signed it over to him on the spot, and the man was so happy he almost cried, Celeste.

He promised to come take his daughter away from my grandmother first thing tomorrow morning. The Imelda chapter is closed." My stomach dropped. "Dominic. You gave him something worth billions?" "It was worth it." "No." | set my hands flat on the counter. "No, that is too much. You worked hard for weeks to acquire that deal, and you just handed it over?" He reached across the island and took my hands, his thumbs stroking over my knuckles. "Listen to me. | would give everything | have, every asset, every company, every last cent, if it guaranteed you a worry- free life.

Money comes back, Celeste. You do not. There is no price tag on the peace of knowing that nothing and no one can stand between us anymore." + "Imelda's father will collect her in the morning. My grandmother will have no reason to interfere. Nothing is standing in the way of our wedding anymore. Not Imelda, not Julian, not anyone. And | would make that trade a hundred times over." | looked at him, at the stubborn set of his jaw and the fierce tenderness in his eyes, and something hot and guilty twisted in my chest. "You are too good to me.

| do not deserve a man who gives away billions just to keep me." "You deserve far more than that." He lifted my hand and pressed a kiss to my knuckles. "And | intend to spend the rest of my life proving it." I smiled at him, and the guilt did not go away. It sat there under the happiness, a small dark stone | would carry for a while. But | let him pull me into his arms, and | let myself believe that everything was finally, truly going to be alright. The next morning, Dominic dropped me off at Helix and left with a kiss and a promise to call.

Later, after lunch with Dominic, | returned to Helix, stood at the balcony of my office with my phone in my hand, waiting for news from Pat. | had sent Kingsley the address before sunrise. I could not call Pat and ask how the party was going, because Pat did not know | was the one who had revealed everything to Kingsley. If she found out before the man had a chance to prove himself, she would only feel betrayed, and | could not risk that. So | waited to hear from her.

It was past noon when | spotted the familiar shape pulling through the gate, and excitement surged through me so fast | nearly dropped my phone. | eventually went down and across the lobby and out through the glass doors, the words already forming in my mouth. 'Pat, tell me everything and leave nothing out.

chapters.title: Chapter 420
chapters.content:
Chapter 420 And then | saw Pat, standing not too far away, and in front of her a woman, tall and striking and dressed like she had stepped out of a magazine, her voice sharp and venomous as she spat words at Pat. Pat stood there with her shoulders squared and her face carefully blank, taking it, the way she always took it, the way she took everything. | knew that face. The recognition hit me like a physical blow, a cold wave that rolled up from the base of my spine and turned the world sharp and still. That face belonged to the branch of the family that had helped destroy my father.

The same jaw, the same cold beautiful cruelty in the eyes, the daughter of the man who had once made my mother weep in the kitchen while my father stood at the window with his hands in his pockets, silent. | had not seen her in years, but | would have known her anywhere. | did not think. | did not plan. | crossed the distance and my hand moved before my mind caught up, and the crack of the slap rang out across the parking lot, loud and clean. The woman's head snapped to the side, and she stumbled back a step, one hand flying to her cheek, her eyes wide with shock and then blazing with fury.

My voice came out low and shaking. "Get off this property before | have you dragged off it." "This is not over." Her voice dropped to a hiss, her eyes moving from me to Pat. "This is definitely not over. Neither of you will get away with this." She turned and walked away, her heels clicking against the pavement, and | stood there with my hands shaking at my sides, my heart pounding so hard | could hear it in my ears. Pat reached for me and pulled me into her arms, and | let her hold me, breathing in the familiar scent of her perfume, grounding myself in the warmth of her.

"lam sorry," Pat murmured. "I did not know she would follow me here." "Itis not your fault." My voice came out steadier than | felt. "It is never your fault." But inside, the anger was already turning over, looking for somewhere to go, and it found Kingsley. He had given Sharon the opportunity to hurt Pat. He had let his past follow him into Pat's present, and now Pat was paying for it. If | had my way, | would have called him right then and told him exactly what | thought of aman who could not keep his own house in order.

And then he showed up, his face tight with anxiety, his eyes fixed on Pat like she was the only thing in the world. The way he looked at Pat, the fear in his eyes, the way his hands hung at his sides like he did not know what to do with them, something in my anger cracked. | had been ready to blame him. But | looked at Pat, at the way her eyes had already found him, at the way she was watching him with a mix of hurt and hope that | recognized all too. Pat wanted this to work. She wanted him to be the man I had heard on the phone last night, the man who had sworn he would not let her down.

And if | let my anger decide for her, | might ruin her one chance at happiness. | might become just another person who took the choice away from her, who told her what she should and should not feel. Pat pulled away from the hug as his voice reached us. Without a single word to him, | turned and walked toward the entrance of Helix, and Pat followed, but | stopped before we reached the door. | turned to face her. "He is not here for me, Pat. He is here for you. Go and speak with him. Know where you both stand." big sale: 100 bonus free fou you

chapters.title: Chapter 421
chapters.content:
Chapter 421 "lam worried about you, Celeste." | softened, the anger draining out of me, leaving only tiredness and a fierce, aching love for this woman who had been my anchor through everything. "| am fine. Go." | went inside and did not look back. But at the top, | paused at the window and watched them.

Pat walking toward him, Kingsley opening the passenger door of his car, the careful way he helped her in, and | whispered more to myself, "Do not disappoint her, Kingsley Duke." The image of Sharon's face stayed with me long after their car had turned the corner and vanished, a splinter | could not work out from under my skin. That smile, that cold beautiful arrogance, the same proud tilt of the jaw | had last seen in the years when my father was still fighting to hold our family together and losing it piece by piece.

| had told myself the past was buried, that the anger had burned itself out the way fires do when there is nothing left to feed them. It had not burned out. It had only been waiting, and one afternoon of Sharon Adams had dragged every ember back to the surface. | forced myself back to my desk and worked through the rest of the day, signing papers | could not have named five minutes later, answering emails on autopilot, because work was the only thing that kept my hands busy and my mind off my mother weeping in the past. | had given up revenge years ago.

| had told myself | was stronger than the people who had hurt us, that walking away was its own kind of victory, and | had believed it right up until the moment | saw Castro Adams's daughter standing in front of Helix. The door swung open and Pat walked in, and the change in her was so complete that | forgot the anger for a second. She was glowing, her cheeks flushed, her eyes bright, the heaviness she had carried out, gone like it had never been there. She held up her bare left hand before | could speak. "| know. No ring.

We're holding on to it." "Pat." "We're dating, Celeste." She said it slowly, like she was tasting the words. "Officially. He asked me to give hima chance, and | said yes." | was across the room before | knew | had moved, and she met me halfway, and we hugged so hard my ribs protested. All the anger, all the worry, all the fear that | had gambled her happiness on a man who might break her again, it all came out of me in one long breath. Every secret | had kept, every risk | had taken to bring them together, it had all been worth it for this. "lam so happy for you, Pat.

| am so, so happy for you." "| feel really happy too." She pulled back, and her eyes were wet. "I don't even understand why | kept pushing him away. | feel so happy, Celeste. And | wish you would stay this happy." "Don't worry about me. Everything will work out in the end. | strongly believe so." She told me about the party then, and | laughed until my eyes watered, the best sound | had made all day, and it chased the shadows out of the room for a while. About Vivian's face when Kingsley walked in carrying enough branded gifts to open a boutique.

About her mother pushing Vivian off her own seat so Kingsley could sit down. About Kingsley kneeling in front of the whole table with a ring worth millions. "So he just showed up?" | asked. "Out of nowhere, in the middle of your sister's birthday?" "Celeste, he proposed to me in front of my entire family. My mother called me perfect. Perfect. She has never said that word to me in thirty years of my life."

chapters.title: Chapter 422
chapters.content:
Chapter 422 "And Vivian?" "| thought she was going to choke on her own cake." I laughed again, and for a moment the afternoon felt like it had never happened, like Sharon Adams was nothing but a bad dream. "You were the one who told him everything, weren't you? " She narrowed her eyes at me. | raised a hand. "| only nudged him in the right direction. Everything else was all him." "Thank you for always having my back." "That's what friends are for.

True friends." She said she still had work in the lab and told me to rest, but | refused, and we went down together and worked until the light outside turned amber and then grey, until the parking lot emptied and the evening went dark. We were still smiling when we walked out of Helix, Pat's car pulling out behind mine, both of us heading for Dominic's place. We had barely reached the road when they showed up. Recognition hit me like a wave of ice water. Castro Adams. Sharon's father. The man who had tried to tear my family apart.

He was older now, heavier, but the eyes were the same, and they were fixed on me with that old cold amusement, the certainty of a man who had never paid for anything he had done. He and his family of supporters had gotten away with it back then, and now he stood in front of me using that history as a point of reference, as a promise of what he could do again. | had underestimated their disregard for the law. | would not make that mistake twice. In that moment, | understood there was no one alive | hated more.

Pat's door opened, and she came to stand beside me, because | was already out of my car, and my stun gun was in my hand. | held it low against my thigh where they could not see it. Castro looked at me, and his voice was calm, almost pleasant. "You raised your hand to my princess, Celeste. Do you have a death wish?" | did not answer. | was watching his men fan out, counting them, measuring distances, looking for the gap Pat could slip through if it came to that. "It wasn't just Celeste." Sharon's voice dripped with venom.

"She and that good-for-nothing ugly friend of hers ganged up on me." Castro smiled, and it was the worst thing | had seen all day. "You want history to repeat itself, Celeste? You've forgotten how | dealt with your family in the past, right? Now I'm going to teach you a lesson you will never forget. And then you will know that no one messes with my princess and gets away with it." He gestured to his men. "Guys. Get them." The men moved, and | stepped fully in front of Pat, my thumb on the trigger of the stun gun, my mind already working.

| could take down the first one, maybe the second, and in the confusion she could run, could get back into her car and drive, and that was all that mattered. Her and the baby. | would not let Castro Adams lay a hand on her. "Stay behind me," | said, low and quiet. "The moment! move, you run. Do not look back." "Celeste..." The men were closing in, and | braced myself, and then a gunshot ripped through the night, fired into the air, and every man froze. | turned, and one of my bodyguards was standing twenty feet away, arms outstretched, a gun in his hands that | had never seen before.

| had watched those men shadow me for weeks, and in all that time | had never once seen them carry a weapon. | stared at the gun like it had appeared from thin air, because as far as | had known, it had. "If you do not disappear right now," the bodyguard said, his voice flat and calm, "the next bullet | release will be embedded in one of your bodies."

chapters.title: Chapter 423
chapters.content:
Chapter 423 Castro laughed, loud and ugly. "Are you threatening me? There are more than twenty of us and one of you. How many can you shoot before we tear you apart? Men, charge! Avenge my daughter! Your pay will doubled!" The men surged forward again, and the bodyguard did not hesitate. He fired once, and the man running at the front, the one closest to me, screamed and went down, clutching his leg, the knife spinning out of his hand and clattering across the asphalt. The men stopped. Some of them backed away.

And then another shot rang out from above us, and Castro cried out and pitched forward onto the ground, his right leg crumpling under him. | looked up, and there, at the top of the Helix building, a figure was barely visible against the dark sky, a rifle glinting in the floodlights. More shots came down after that, one after another, each one finding a leg, and men fell like dominoes, crying out, clutching their thighs. The ones still standing broke and ran, some of them leaving their cars behind, some of them dragging their wounded into the remaining vehicles.

Sharon was already inside the lead car, | realized, had been since the first shot, and when two men hauled Castro into the back seat and the car tore away, she did not look back once. When the last car had disappeared, the silence rushed back in, and | realized my hand was shaking around the stun gun. | lowered it, pressed it against my thigh, and turned to the bodyguard who had stayed beside me. "Who shot all those men? Who was on the roof?" "That was my partner." He nodded toward the building.

" The moment we saw the armed men, he took the sniper rifle from our car and climbed up to the roof of Helix for a vantage point. | stayed down here to make sure nothing got past him." "1 never knew you carried guns." "We are ex-military, ma'am. Licensed bodyguards, licensed weapons. We have carried them the whole time we have been assigned to you. We simply never had a reason to show them before tonight." | looked at the empty road, at the knives and sticks scattered across the asphalt, at the dark stains already soaking into the tarmac. "Thank you.

| do not know what would have happened if you had not been here." "Itis my job, ma'am." "And I need one more thing from you. Do not tell Dominic about any of this." He studied me for a moment, then nodded. "As you wish." | turned to Pat, who was standing by her car with her arms wrapped around herself, her face pale in the streetlight. "Are you alright? Do you need a doctor?" She shook her head. "I'm fine. It's just a little shocking to see so many people get shot up close." | crossed to her and pulled her into my arms, and she let me hold her, her breath shaky against my shoulder.

"| am sorry. | am so sorry you had to see that." "It's not your fault, Celeste." It was, though. Every bit of it was. Castro Adams had not come for Pat. He had come for me, for the debt he believed my family still owed his, and Pat had only been in the way. Dominic had spent the past month solving my problems one after another, shielding me from my past. This one was mine. | held Pat tighter and made myself a promise: | would finish what my family never could. | would put Castro Adams where he belonged. "| need to go back inside," | said, pulling back.

"The cameras around the building must have captured everything. | am going to copy the footage." "What are you going to do with it?" I looked at her, and | felt the smile spread across my face, cold and certain. "| am going to send Castro Adams to prison."

chapters.title: Chapter 424
chapters.content:
Chapter 424 Back inside, the security room felt too quiet, the screens glowing blue in the dark. | pulled up the feed and watched it twice, Castro stepping out of the car, Sharon beside him, his men fanning out, the shots, the men falling, Castro dragged into the car and driven away. | copied it onto a drive, and then | made the first call. It was a friend from college who was now a detective. He picked up on the second ring, his voice rough with sleep. "Celeste. This is a surprise." "lam reporting a crime, Officer.

Attempted kidnapping, assault, and a public disturbance involving more than twenty armed men outside Helix Laboratory." There was a long pause. "Are you alright?" "1 am. | have footage. | am sending it to you now." "Send it. We can meet tomorrow to talk about the case." "1 will be there." | sent the footage, then | made the second call, to the best criminal lawyer | knew. He answered on the first ring. "Miss. Adams. It is late. What is wrong?" After we exchanged pleasantries, | went straight to the point. "| need you to take on a case. | am sending you a video.

| want the people in it charged and brought to court. I'd like to meet with you tomorrow." "Send it over. What time tomorrow?" "Nine in the morning. | will come to your office." "| will be ready." | ended the call and stood in the security room for a long moment, the drive warm in my hand. When Castro Adams finally stood in front of a judge, | would be there to watch. Pat was waiting by the cars when | came out, steadier now, some color back in her cheeks. We got in, the bodyguards fell in behind us, and we drove the rest of the way to Dominic's place in silence.

The whole way, | kept thinking about the child Pat was carrying and the man who had almost put his hands on her tonight. Castro Adams thought he had come to teach me a lesson. He had not. He had only given me a reason. | kept the smile on the whole drive home. | rehearsed it in the rearview mirror the way other people rehearsed speeches, adjusting the corners until it looked natural, until it reached my eyes, because Dominic would know the difference in a second and | could not afford to let him see.

My knuckles were white around the steering wheel and my jaw ached, but by the time | pulled into the driveway and found him waiting in the doorway with that soft, expectant look he wore every time he looked at me, the smile had almost stopped being an act. Then Pat's car pulled in behind mine. "Finally," Dominic said, meeting me at the door. He took my bag, kissed my temple, and looked past me at Pat with genuine warmth. "I was starting to think you two had moved into the lab." "Almost did." Pat rubbed her arms against the night air. " Your woman is a machine. | had to drag her out of there.

"Lucky for me she listens to someone." | laughed, and it sounded almost real. "| listen to no one. | was hungry." "Then you are in luck." He swung an arm around my shoulder and steered me inside. The house was warm, all soft amber light and the smell of tomatoes, and | let myself sink into it. | sat at the marble island and let Dominic serve me, let him fuss over portions and complain that | was not eating enough, and | answered every question about my day with a lie wrapped in a smile. Good. Productive. The usual. Pat watched me twice.

She frowned at me, but she played along anyway, and | loved her for it. "You are quiet tonight," Dominic said, settling onto the stool beside me with his own plate.

chapters.title: Chapter 425
chapters.content:
Chapter 425 "lam eating." | gestured with my fork. "Talking and chewing is how people choke, Dominic." "See, this is why | eat alone." Pat laughed into her glass. "He has a point. You almost took out an entire bakery with that croissant story last week." "The croissant story is important. It has layers." "Like you," Dominic said, deadpan, and | threw a piece of bread at him. He caught it, bit into it, and grinned at me with such unguarded happiness that my chest squeezed.

This was the part | could not fake and could not explain, the way he looked at me, like | was the answer to a question he had been asking his whole life. Every time | saw it | wanted to tell him everything, wanted to crawl into his lap and cry until the poison was out of me. But Dominic had already carried enough of my weight, and this was mine, the debt my family had never been able to collect, and I would collect it alone.

So | smiled and | joked, | fed him strawberries while Pat pretended to be scandalized, | laughed until my cheeks hurt, and when the night finally wound down and Pat yawned her way upstairs, | stood at the kitchen window with my hands in the sink and watched my reflection waver in the dark glass. "Coming to bed?" Dominic's arms wrapped around me from behind. "In a minute." He kissed the back of my neck and left me there, and | stood until the water ran cold, thinking about a lot of things. | do not remember falling asleep. I remember the dream. | was small.

Nine, maybe ten, small enough that the world was made of adult waists and door handles that reached my chin. We were in the new house, the one my father had worked hard to buy after he lost everything, the one with the yellow walls my mother had painted herself and the bare garden where she said we would plant roses in the spring. Then the door came off its hinges. Men poured through it, so many of them, sticks and knives in their fists, and they did not look at me.

They moved past me like | was furniture, and that was the most frightening part, that | was so small | did not even register as a person to them. Castro walked in behind them like a man arriving at a party, his arms folded across his chest, his wife Annabelle at his side in a fur coat that brushed the floor. Behind them came Sharon, younger than me, with a smile | would spend years learning to recognize, and a boy with their father's cold eyes. Caspian. | knew his name long before | ever knew his face.

My father came out of the kitchen, and he did not get three steps before the first stick came down across his back. He fell. The men closed around him, and | heard the sound, the wet, rhythmic sound of wood meeting flesh, over and over, and | could not move, could not breathe, could only stand against the wall and watch. My mother came running, eight months pregnant, her hands flying to her mouth, and one of the men shoved her.

She went down hard, her cry cutting through everything, and then there was blood, a dark bloom spreading across the pale fabric of her dress, and | ran for her, | was running, | was going to reach her, and then the boy, Caspian, stepped into my path and pushed me. | went down on the tiles, my palms scraping raw, and before | could get up Sharon was standing over me, younger than me, her face twisting into ugly shapes, making faces at me while | cried, laughing while my mother bled.

Felix had slipped out the back, | learned that later, had run barefoot to the neighbors' houses until someone finally listened. But in that moment | did not know it. In that moment all | knew was my mother on the floor and my father on the floor and blood on the tiles and a girl my age laughing at my tears.

chapters.title: Chapter 426
chapters.content:
Chapter 426 My father fought his way up. He got his feet under him somehow, bleeding from a dozen places, and he lurched toward my mother, and he fell again, and that was the fall that took half his body. The stroke found him there on the floor of our ruined house, and when they finally lifted him up, the left side of his face had gone slack and his arm hung like something that did not belong to him. Castro stood over them. He stood over my mother and my father, and he said the words | have never been able to unhear, the words that live in the space behind my ribs to this day.

"Before me, you are all nothing. If | wanted, | could kill every one of you and nothing would happen to me, because | have money and you have nothing." It was the same money that used to belong to my father. His whole family watched, smiling. Then help came. The neighbors Felix had roused, the police, someone, everyone, and my mother and father were rushed to the hospital, and we followed. They would not let me stay in my mother's hospital room.

Felix and | were left in our father's hospital room, where he lay unable to walk, unable to speak half his words, his eyes fixed on the ceiling like he was counting the hours he had left. | heard a nurse saying my mother was about to give birth. | thought of the day before, when | had asked my mother when | would finally see my baby sister. She had let me rub her belly and I had felt the little kicks against my palm, and she had laughed and told me one more month, just one more month. | had already prepared her gifts. A yellow blanket. A stuffed rabbit with floppy ears.

| had hidden them under my bed and | had imagined her face, imagined her small hands, imagined the way she would smell. I left my father's room. The doctors and nurses would not let me in to see my mother, so | waited until they were busy, until the corridor emptied, and | slipped through the door of the delivery room. No one noticed me. They were all crowded around the bed, my mother straining and crying, the doctors shouting numbers | did not understand, and | pressed myself into the corner behind the curtain and | watched.

| watched my mother push, watched her face go red and terrible, watched the doctor catch the baby. My mother had told me that all babies were supposed to cry when they were born. But my sister did not cry. She came out silent and blue, and the room went quiet in a way that was worse than any scream, and | saw the doctor's face, saw the nurse's face, saw my mother's eyes roll back as she fainted, and | screamed. | screamed from my hiding place, and the doctors finally saw me, finally noticed the child in the corner, and one of them rushed at me, and | fainted before they could catch me.

| lost my sister that night. My father lost the use of his legs, and then the rest of himself, and my mother almost died, and the joy in our family died with the baby, and nothing was ever the same. My mother fought for justice afterward. She filed reports and hired lawyers and sat in courtrooms, and one by one the doors closed in her face, because the system fails people like us when the people across from them have money and names, and Castro had both, and we had neither.

He came to our house one more time, Sharon on his hip, and he laughed and told my mother this was only the beginning, and then he left, and my mother stood at the window with her hands in her pockets and said nothing. Then Castro's wife, Annabelle died. In childbirth, with twin sons who never took a breath, and | watched my mother's face when she heard, watched something move behind her eyes, and she said it was nature's way of delivering justice, and | believed her.

| believed karma had finally reached out and put its hand on that family, and | carried that belief in my chest for years like a talisman.

chapters.title: Chapter 427
chapters.content:
Chapter 427 My father never recovered. He lived for a few more years, lived sideways, one arm useless, one leg dragging, his eyes on a middle distance where the man he had been still stood, and then he died quietly in his sleep, and | remember feeling relieved, and then hating myself for it, because he had been gone for so long already. The sticks had taken him and the stroke had finished it, and what was left had only been waiting for permission to stop. My mother buried him, and then she sat Felix and me down and told us that hate was a poison we could not afford.
